title: Can AI speed up due diligence on add-on acquisitions?
description: AI in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) diligence: what AI reads first and what your team decides. Plus tool prices and our count of merger agreements naming AI.
industry: Acquisitive companies, platforms and holding companies
verdict: AI reads the seller's data room first and flags issues; your deal team, lawyers and accountants still judge[^15][^5].
Most surveyed large acquirers and private equity firms already use AI in diligence, mainly on legal agreements[^2][^45].
Expect errors: legal research AI hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time in testing, so check every flag[^6][^11].
Check the target's own AI too: 37.9% of the 2026 public merger agreements we counted mention "artificial intelligence"[^1][^19].
Keep the seller's files inside the data room, or in an AI tool your counsel has cleared[^15][^5].

summary: AI due diligence uses AI to read a target's data room first, pulling contract terms, numbers and gaps with page cites[^15][^16]. It changes speed and coverage, so your team checks more and asks the seller better questions[^2][^30]. Human checking of every flag makes or breaks it[^6].
humanRole: Head of corporate development: owns the scope, the request list and the go/no-go call. Surveyed acquirers rank doing more diligence in the time available as AI's top goal[^2].

Controller: ties every number AI pulls to the target's trial balance and working-capital schedule. Post-closing price adjustments are nearly universal in private-target deals, and working capital is the most common measure[^17][^39].

Outside counsel: checks AI output for accuracy, then signs legal findings and the disclosure schedule. Under American Bar Association (ABA) Opinion 512, lawyers using AI keep their duties of competence and confidentiality[^5].
Compliance lead: decides whether to disclose misconduct found at the target. The Department of Justice (DOJ) safe harbor needs disclosure within six months of closing[^9][^10].
teamAfter: Deal leads move from first reads to follow-up questions for the seller and management interviews. Surveyed acquirers rank doing more diligence in the time first, and headcount reduction last[^2].
Counsel can cover more contracts, because AI fills the contract grid first and links each answer to its source[^23][^30].
Corporate development starts the integration plan earlier: acquirers now use AI to size a target's cost base from public sources before bidding[^4].
Headcount isn't the goal: only 2% of AI-using firms report AI-related employment decreases, and about 96% see no change in employment[^12][^13].

example.input: Illustrative, not a client result: a 150-person heating and cooling services platform is buying a smaller add-on. The seller's data room holds customer contracts, leases, 36 months of trial balances, payroll and insurance policies. The buyer has a standard request list.
example.output: A contract grid with term, auto-renewal, consent needed on a change of owner, and price increase clauses, each with a page cite[^15][^23]. A check of 36 months of working capital and a gap list against the request list[^17][^16]. The controller, counsel and corporate development check each flag, then send the seller questions.

recipes.name: 1. A few add-ons a year, a small deal team
recipes.when: A few deals a year, a deal team of a few people, and sellers whose data rooms already have AI built in[^20][^21].
flow: Counsel: clear the non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and the AI tool's retention terms before any file goes in
Corporate development lead: load the request list and the data-room index
AI: compare the room with the request list and draft a gap list with page cites
Controller: tie every number AI pulls to the target's trial balance
Counsel: read every change-of-control and assignment hit
Corporate development lead: turn gaps into seller questions and the go/no-go memo
recipes.cost: Claude Team lists at $20 to $25 per member a month, read 26 Nov 2026[^26]. By our math, five seats cost $1,200 to $1,500 a year, plus the seller's room AI[^20].

recipes.name: 2. Several add-ons a year on one playbook
recipes.when: Several deals a year run on the same checklist, where your past issue lists are the edge[^20].
flow: Corporate development lead: write the standard request list, prompts and issue-list format once
Counsel: approve which AI assistant may connect to data rooms
AI: work inside each room through the vendor's connector, under the room's permissions
Controller: run the same working-capital check on every deal
Counsel: sign legal findings and the disclosure-schedule questions
COO: carry flagged issues into the integration plan
recipes.cost: Data rooms price per deal or by data volume and users[^20][^21]. Claude Team seats list at $20 a member a month billed yearly, read 26 Nov 2026[^26].

recipes.name: 3. Hundreds of similar contracts in one room
recipes.when: Customer, supplier or lease contracts number in the hundreds, and change-of-control consents decide the deal[^23].
flow: Counsel: pick the clause fields to extract
AI: fill a contract grid with each answer linked to its source page
Counsel: check every hit and a sample of blanks
Controller: tie contract values to revenue by customer
Corporate development lead: price the consents needed before closing
recipes.cost: Kira and Hebbia publish no price, so expect a demo and a quote[^23][^24]. The review usually runs through counsel's own bill.

ownData.title: How often do public merger agreements mention AI?
ownData.intro: We searched SEC EDGAR full text on 26 Nov 2026, one calendar year at a time, in 8-K current reports[^1]. We counted documents with the phrase "Company Disclosure Letter", a marker of public-target merger agreements[^1]. Then we counted those that also say "artificial intelligence", and 110 of 2026's 111 hits are the merger agreement itself[^1].
ownData.note: Counts documents, not deals, so amendments can double count, and private add-on agreements are rarely filed[^1]. A mention is not always a full AI clause: we read only two by hand[^18][^19]. Other wordings, such as "Disclosure Schedule", are missed.

rules.name: Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) thresholds for 2026
rules.what: A deal must be worth at least $133.9M before a premerger filing is needed[^31]. Filing fees run from $35,000 to $2,460,000[^31]. Most add-ons bought by a 40-500 person company fall below the threshold.

rules.name: Expanded HSR filing form
rules.what: A federal court vacated the 2025 form, and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) accepts the older form again[^32]. Check the current form before you file.

rules.name: 2023 Merger Guidelines
rules.what: The FTC and DOJ confirmed in Feb 2025 that the 2023 guidelines frame merger review[^33].

rules.name: DOJ M&A Safe Harbor Policy
rules.status: In force, kept in the March 2026 policy
rules.what: Disclose misconduct found at the target within six months of closing, and fix it within a year, for a presumption the DOJ won't prosecute[^9][^10]. Faster diligence leaves more of that clock for the legal call.

rules.name: DOJ Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs
rules.what: Prosecutors expect thorough diligence on acquisition targets[^8]. They also ask whether a company manages risks from AI[^47].

rules.name: ABA Formal Opinion 512
rules.what: Lawyers using generative AI keep their duties of competence and confidentiality, including knowing the tool's risks[^5]. Ask counsel how their tools treat seller data.

rules.name: FTC orders to delete algorithms
rules.what: The FTC has ordered companies to delete models built from unlawfully obtained data[^34][^43]. A buyer takes on that risk with the target's models.

rules.name: SEC actions on AI-washing
rules.what: The SEC penalized two advisers $400,000 in total for claiming AI they did not use[^35]. Presto Automation was charged over how it described its voice AI[^36].

rules.name: EU AI Act, as amended by the Digital Omnibus
rules.what: Matters if the target sells or uses AI in the European Union[^37]. Hiring, credit and education uses face high-risk duties from 2 Dec 2027[^37].

howToTest: Record today's numbers on your last closed deal: deal-team hours, days to the issue list, and issues found after signing.
Rerun that closed deal's data room through the tool, since you already know the answers.
Score each finding as found, missed or false, with the page it cites. Vals scored tools against a lawyer baseline on the same tasks[^7].
Count hallucinations, not just hits: the Stanford-led study scored answers correct, incomplete or hallucinated[^6].
Check every hit against its cited page, as NIST's generative AI profile suggests for sources and citations[^11].
Run a sample of the free CUAD and MAUD test sets for a public baseline[^28][^29].

Price the lift: hours saved, plus each issue found before signing, valued at the price cut or claim it would have cost. Nearly three in ten private deals see an indemnity claim, and median escrow is 10% of deal value[^38][^39].
Decide with counsel and the controller to keep, change or stop.
watchOuts: Confident wrong answers: commercial legal research tools hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time in a preregistered test[^6]. Require a page cite for every finding, and have a person check each one[^11].
Strong at answering questions, weak at markup: lawyers beat every tool at redlining, 79.7 to at most 65.0, in the Vals benchmark[^7]. Keep contract markup with counsel.
Leaking the seller's data: exporting data-room files to an outside AI tool creates uncontrolled copies (Datasite's view, vendor)[^15]. Check the NDA and the tool's retention terms first[^5].
Buying overstated AI: Presto did not tell investors that its voice AI ran on a third party's technology[^36]. Ask the target for usage logs, vendor contracts and human-help rates.
Buying a model you must delete: FTC orders made Everalbum and Rite Aid delete algorithms[^43][^48]. Ask how each model's training data was collected and what consent covers it.
Cutting diligence because AI is fast: acquirers that did less diligence saw weaker post-deal results and more goodwill write-downs[^14]. Spend the saved time on deeper checks.

faq.a: Only as a first pass, because AI reads and flags while people check and decide[^30][^5]. Legal research AI tools hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time in a preregistered test[^6].

faq.q: How is AI used in M&A due diligence?
faq.a: Large acquirers use AI most often to review legal agreements, manage workstreams and review financial statements[^2]. In one 2026 survey of large serial acquirers, 79% used it on legal agreements[^2].

faq.q: Will AI replace due diligence jobs?
faq.a: No, the evidence points to help rather than job loss: only 2% of AI-using US firms report AI-related employment decreases[^12]. About 96% of AI-using firms report no change in employment[^13]. In M&A, surveyed acquirers rank headcount reduction last among AI goals[^2].

faq.q: Is it safe to put data-room files into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Only after counsel checks the NDA and the tool's retention terms, because lawyers must keep client information confidential[^5]. OpenAI says ChatGPT Business data is never used for training (vendor)[^25]. Datasite warns that exporting files creates uncontrolled copies (vendor)[^15].

faq.q: How much does AI due diligence software cost?
faq.a: General AI seats list at $20 to $25 per member a month for Claude Team and $21 for the Copilot add-on, read 26 Nov 2026[^26][^27]. Data-room AI is quoted per deal, and contract-review tools such as Kira publish no price[^20][^21][^23].

faq.q: What does due diligence on a target's own AI check?
faq.a: Diligence on a target's AI checks how it uses AI, who owns AI-made work, and whether its AI policies hold up[^19][^18]. Our count found 111 public merger-agreement documents mentioning "artificial intelligence" from 1 Jan to 25 Nov 2026[^1].

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy the tools: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are now bought rather than built, up from 53% in 2024[^40]. For a few deals a year, the seller's room AI plus business AI seats is enough[^20][^26].
buyVsBuild.build: Build the playbook, not the software: your request list, prompts and issue-list format, run the same way every deal[^20]. Data rooms now let your approved assistant work inside the room (Datasite, vendor)[^15].

pickElse: You need earnings checked, not files read: get a quality-of-earnings (QoE) report, which vets normalized earnings and working capital[^41]. AI can prepare the data for it.
To shift the risk: representations and warranties insurance (RWI) was referenced in 63% of private-target deals in the ABA's 2025 study, up from 55%[^42].
One deal in a seller's room: use the room's own AI, such as Datasite Blueflame or the Intralinks assistant, before building anything[^16][^21].
Hundreds of similar contracts: a contract-review tool such as Litera Kira, with 1,400+ pre-built fields (vendor), run through counsel[^23].

answers.human-role: Your team keeps every judgment: corporate development owns the deal call, the controller checks the numbers, and counsel signs legal findings[^2][^5].
answers.team-after: Your deal team moves from first reads to seller questions, full contract review and earlier integration planning[^2][^4].
answers.example: The seller's data room goes in, and a cited contract grid, a working-capital check and a gap list come out for your team to check[^15][^16].
answers.table-1: General AI seats cost $20 to $25 per user a month, while data-room and contract-review tools quote per deal or publish no price[^26][^27][^20]. Prices come from each vendor's own page.
answers.table-2: AI tools beat lawyers at answering document questions and at summaries, while lawyers beat every tool at redlining and filing research[^7].
answers.table-3: Between 21% and 93% of surveyed acquirers use AI in M&A work, depending on who was asked and when[^44][^2].
answers.recipes: Start with AI seats and the seller's room AI if you buy a few add-ons a year, a shared playbook for several, or a contract-review tool for hundreds of contracts[^26][^20][^23].
answers.own-data: More often each year: 37.9% of the 2026 public merger agreements we counted mention "artificial intelligence", up from 0.5% in 2019[^1]. Check the target's own AI as part of diligence[^18].
answers.rules: Antitrust filing rules, the DOJ safe harbor, lawyers' ethics rules on AI, and federal and EU rules on a target's own AI all apply[^31][^9][^5][^34]. None of this is legal advice.
answers.benchmark: Rerun your last closed deal's data room through the tool, score every finding as found, missed or false, then price the time and issues it saved[^7][^6].
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI-assisted diligence goes wrong through confident wrong answers, leaked seller files, overstated AI at the target, and diligence cut short because AI was fast[^6][^15][^36][^14].
answers.buy-or-build: Buy the tools and build the playbook: your request list, prompts and issue-list format, run the same way on every deal[^40][^20].
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you need earnings checked, want to insure the risk, have one deal in a seller's room, or face hundreds of similar contracts[^41][^42].

offer.heading: Is your deal team still reading every data-room file by hand? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Walk us through your request list and your last add-on's data room. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step for your next deal, a before-and-after measure and what counsel should clear first. You get it in writing, with no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Dana (COO): clear on who does what and how to measure before and after on a closed deal. Tripped on 'hallucinated' in the bottom line; now 'gave wrong answers'. Recipe 2 gives the COO the hand-off of flagged issues into the integration plan, which links to the post-merger integration guide in related pages.

Ops head: jargon in the example and rules ('tie-out', 'price escalators', 'change-of-control consent', 'presumption of declination'). Now a working-capital check, price increase clauses, consent needed on a change of owner, and a presumption the DOJ won't prosecute. Every recipe step names a role.

GM: wanted the payoff in money, not just hours. The test step now values each issue found before signing at the price cut or claim it would have cost, next to the indemnity-claim and escrow figures. Pilot path is clear: rerun one closed deal first.

Head of corporate development: roles match how a deal runs (corp dev owns the call, controller the numbers, counsel the legal sign-off, compliance the 180-day clock). Cut invented deal-count thresholds from recipes 1 and 2 ('two or three', 'four or more'); now 'a few' and 'several'. Source checker: confirm the Vals lawyer baselines (70.1 for both document Q&A and EDGAR research).

Steve: wanted a plain dollar figure for a small team; recipe 1 now says five users cost $1,200 to $1,500 a year at list. Security worry answered in the bottom line and FAQ 4. No Zavient price, per site rules; the offer promises the first step and a before-and-after measure in writing, with no sales pitch.
